name: Prince Edward Island
summary_text: Prince Edward Island stands under the national framework of Canada. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No jurisdiction in Canada restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, and entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers. Federal criminal law and human-rights protections apply in Prince Edward Island as they do across the country.  Legal gender recognition in Prince Edward Island carries no surgery requirement. A 2016 amendment to the Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement and replaced it with a declaration of the gender the applicant identifies with, supported by a letter from a doctor. The regime has operated on that basis ever since. An adult born in the province may apply if resident there for at least three months; the application requires completed forms including a physician statement and a written statement by the applicant, signed before a commissioner of oaths at Vital Statistics.  Provincial photo ID can carry a non-binary or undisclosed marker. Since 4 December 2018 Islanders completing a driver's licence at Access PEI locations may select 'gender not listed', shown on the licence as X, or 'prefer not to say', shown as a blank, alongside male and female. The Government of Prince Edward Island stated that the province was the first jurisdiction in Canada to offer the 'prefer not to say' blank option.  National police-reported hate-crime data gives no Prince Edward Island figure. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, up 1% on 2023, at a rate of 12.1 per 100,000 population, down 2% in 2024 and up 142% since 2018, with eight provinces recording stable or declining rates. The release reports no Prince Edward Island-specific rate or incident count, and no provincially deviating pattern is documented for the province.

name: Quebec
summary_text: Quebec is a province of Canada and stands under the national framework: gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Federal criminal law and the federal human-rights framework apply uniformly in Quebec. No jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, federal identity documents can carry an X marker, and entry carries no trans-specific friction.  Provincial law adds a second layer. Quebec's Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms has listed gender identity and gender expression as prohibited grounds of discrimination since 2016, and the enforcement machinery produces outcomes: on 10 June 2024 the Quebec Human Rights Tribunal found that a Montreal bar discriminated against a trans woman in hiring on the basis of her gender identity and ordered the employer to pay $10,000 in moral damages, $4,000 in punitive damages and $118.40 for unpaid training. A trans visitor considering employment or service refusal in Quebec can point to a tribunal that has ruled this way in the recent past.  The province's rules on sex designation and identity documents were reshaped by litigation. After a two-month trial heard in front of 29 witnesses, the Quebec Superior Court held in 2021 QCCS 191 that provisions of the Civil Code of Quebec were invalid because they violated the fundamental rights of trans, intersex and non-binary people; the Quebec Court of Appeal largely upheld that decision in 2024 QCCA 348, and the ruling led to legislative reform of the Civil Code. Documents issued under the reformed regime should therefore reflect a visitor's stated sex designation, though the specific issuing practice in Quebec is not set out in the sources.  Correctional placement is the one area where Quebec has moved against the national direction. On 19 June 2025 CBC News reported that the Quebec public security minister announced that transgender inmates in the province will be incarcerated according to their anatomical sex rather than their gender identity, citing fairness and safety, in a directive issued just after trans woman Levana Ballouz sought a transfer to a women's prison following her conviction for murdering her partner and children. Advocates stated that the policy violates the Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. This affects a transit visitor only in the event of detention, but it is a documented reversal of the previous practice of considering gender identity in correctional placement.  National crime data does not isolate Quebec. Statistics Canada reported 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents nationally in 2024, a 1% rise on 2023, at a rate of 12.1 per 100,000 residents, down 2% over the year but up 142% since 2018. Provincial rates ranged from 5.3 per 100,000 in Manitoba and Newfoundland and Labrador to 16.0 in Ontario, with eight provinces stable or declining. No Quebec-specific rate appears in the release.
